name: Sun
description: The Sun is a yellow dwarf star that sits at the centre of our Solar System and provides the energy necessary for life on Earth. Its gravity holds the entire system together, keeping everything from the largest planets to the smallest debris in orbit. As a massive ball of glowing gas, it accounts for more than 99 percent of the total mass of the Solar System.
ou_involvement: The Open University studies how the solar wind interacts with Earth's magnetic field through the ESA–CAS SMILE mission, whose X-ray camera detectors were developed and tested at the OU's Centre for Electronic Imaging. How particles from the Sun damage the cameras and detectors on spacecraft is a core research area for the Centre, which tests detectors against space radiation for missions across the Solar System.

name: Mercury
description: Mercury is the smallest planet in our solar system and the closest to the Sun, resulting in extreme temperature variations. Its heavily cratered surface resembles Earth's Moon, indicating that the planet has been geologically quiet for billions of years. Despite its small size, it has a global magnetic field, which is surprising for such a small planet, and a high density that suggests a massive metallic core.
ou_involvement: OU scientists have spent decades studying Mercury’s surface composition to understand the early volcanic history of the planet. Researchers use advanced spectroscopy to interpret data from visiting spacecraft and map the distribution of chemical elements. An OU scientist is the UK lead for BepiColombo's MIXS X-ray spectrometer, which will map the elements on Mercury's surface.

name: BepiColombo
description: BepiColombo is a joint mission between ESA and JAXA that is due to enter orbit around Mercury on 21 November 2026. The mission utilizes two separate orbiters to perform the most comprehensive study of the planet's surface, composition, and magnetic field to date. By mapping the planet at various wavelengths, scientists aim to solve the mystery of Mercury's oversized core and its unique geological evolution.
ou_involvement: OU academics are members of BepiColombo's M-CAM monitoring camera team, analysing images returned during the spacecraft's Mercury flybys. The Open University was also a development partner, alongside instrument lead the University of Leicester, in building the Mercury Imaging X-ray Spectrometer (MIXS).

name: Venus
description: Venus is often called Earth’s twin due to its similar size and density, but it possesses a thick, toxic atmosphere that creates a runaway greenhouse effect. The planet rotates backwards on its axis and suffers from surface temperatures hot enough to melt lead. Its surface is hidden by thick clouds of sulfuric acid, which are only penetrable by radar and specialized spectrometers.
ou_involvement: The Open University is helping to prepare ESA's EnVision mission to Venus. With a £2.3 million ESA grant, an OU team leads the testing and characterisation of the detectors in the VenSpec-U ultraviolet spectrometer, which will study the sulphur chemistry of Venus's clouds, and takes part in science preparations for the mission.

name: Earth
description: Earth is the only known planet to support life and is characterized by its vast oceans and nitrogen-oxygen atmosphere. It features a dynamic surface shaped by plate tectonics and an active climate system that regulates temperatures for its diverse ecosystems. Our home planet sits within the Sun's habitable zone, allowing water to exist in liquid form on the surface.
ou_involvement: The Open University uses Earth observation data to monitor environmental changes and support international climate conservation efforts. Academics develop machine learning algorithms to analyse satellite imagery for tracking deforestation, urban growth, and glacial retreat. This research provides a critical foundation for teaching students about the intersection of technology and environmental sustainability.

name: ISS
description: The International Space Station is a modular research laboratory that orbits the Earth and serves as a home for international crews. It provides a unique microgravity environment where scientists can conduct experiments that would be impossible on the ground. The station is a symbol of international cooperation, involving space agencies from the United States, Russia, Europe, Japan, and Canada.
ou_involvement: OU scientists took part in the DLR-led BIOlogy and Mars Experiment (BIOMEX) aboard the ISS's EXPOSE-R2 facility, mounted outside the Zvezda module, exposing bacteria, algae, lichens and fungi to the vacuum, UV radiation and temperature extremes of space for about 18 months. The samples returned to Earth with British astronaut Tim Peake in June 2016, and results helped assess whether such organisms (and, by extension, life on Mars) could survive interplanetary transfer.

name: Hubble
description: Hubble is one of NASA's most successful space telescopes and has spent over three decades providing iconic images of the deep universe. It orbits above the Earth's atmosphere to capture clear views of galaxies, nebulae, and planets without the distortion caused by our air. The mission has fundamentally changed our understanding of the age of the universe and the existence of dark energy.
ou_involvement: OU astronomers actively use Hubble's extensive archive to research stellar populations and the evolution of distant galaxies, work that also feeds directly into the university's astronomy curriculum. The high-performance CCDs in Hubble's WFC3 camera are built by Teledyne e2v, the same UK manufacturer that partners closely with the OU's Centre for Electronic Imaging on the characterisation and radiation-hardening of space CCDs.

name: Sentinel-2
description: Sentinel-2 is a constellation of satellites, currently three, designed to provide high-resolution optical imagery for the European Copernicus program. The mission monitors Earth's land surfaces to provide data on vegetation, soil, and water cover for environmental and security monitoring. Its frequent revisit time allows for the tracking of rapid changes such as agricultural growth or natural disasters.

name: Sentinel-3
description: Sentinel-3 is a multi-instrument mission intended to provide high-accuracy data for ocean and land monitoring. It measures sea-surface topography, ocean temperature, and land-surface colour to support ocean forecasting and climate research. The mission is essential for tracking marine pollution and observing the impact of climate change on coastal ecosystems.

name: CASTOR
description: CASTOR is a proposed Canadian-led space telescope designed to perform high-resolution imaging in the ultraviolet and blue-optical wavelengths. It will feature a wide-field view that is significantly larger than Hubble's, enabling it to survey vast portions of the sky. The mission aims to address fundamental questions in cosmology, including the nature of dark energy and the formation of galaxies.
ou_involvement: The CEI at the Open University was awarded £2.1 million to lead testing and space-qualification of the CIS303 and CIS120 UV detectors (built by Teledyne e2v) for CASTOR, a Canadian-led 1-metre UV/optical space telescope targeting launch around 2030. This includes electro-optical testing, optimising the detectors' performance, and measuring how well different UV coatings and enhancement technologies work and how they degrade, to raise the sensors' readiness for spaceflight.

name: TRUTHS
description: TRUTHS is a UK-led mission delivered by ESA that aims to create a 'gold standard' reference point for climate measurements in space. It will measure the Sun's incoming radiation and Earth's reflected radiation with unprecedented accuracy to calibrate other satellites. This high-precision data will significantly increase our confidence in long-term climate change data and environmental forecasting.
ou_involvement: The CEI carries out experimental radiation-damage characterisation of the Teledyne e2v CIS120 CMOS sensor being evaluated for TRUTHS and other next-generation missions, testing dark current, noise and quantum efficiency both before and after gamma and proton irradiation across a range of operating temperatures. This work helps confirm the detector technology can maintain the high calibration accuracy TRUTHS needs throughout a multi-year mission.

name: SMILE
description: The Solar wind Magnetosphere Ionosphere Link Explorer is a collaborative mission between ESA and CAS that launched on 19 May 2026. It is designed to provide the first global images of the Earth's magnetosphere and its dynamic interaction with the solar wind. By observing X-ray emissions, the mission aims to reveal how solar activity impacts our planet's magnetic shield and atmosphere.
ou_involvement: The Centre for Electronic Imaging developed and tested the twin CCD370 detectors (4510×4510-pixel, 18-micron-pixel sensors derived from the CCD270s developed for PLATO) that form the focal plane of SMILE's Soft X-ray Imager (SXI), running noise, charge-transfer-inefficiency and defect-mapping tests before flight. The OU is now part of the mission's operations team, working closely with the SXI team to get the most science from the detectors.

name: Swift
description: Swift is a multi-wavelength space observatory dedicated to detecting and localizing gamma-ray bursts within seconds. It rapidly reorients itself to observe the afterglow of these massive cosmic explosions across X-ray and optical wavelengths. The mission has been operating for over 20 years, contributing significantly to our understanding of black hole formation and neutron star mergers.

name: UKube-1
description: UKube-1 was the first mission commissioned by the UK Space Agency to demonstrate advanced CubeSat technologies in orbit. It served as a way maker for the UK small satellite industry by testing payloads for space weather monitoring and secure communications. The mission provided invaluable hands-on experience for researchers and students across multiple British universities.
ou_involvement: The CEI's Compact CMOS Camera Demonstrator (C3D) flew on UKube-1, the UK Space Agency's first CubeSat, after CEI won one of only three science payload slots. Launched in July 2014, its three cameras achieved the first in-orbit demonstration of a European 0.18-micron CMOS imaging technology, and radiation testing showed the sensor suffered dark-current and flatband-voltage degradation similar to CCDs while also revealing CMOS-specific effects like single-event upsets. This data has since informed the design of more radiation-tolerant space CMOS sensors.

name: Moon
description: The Moon is Earth's only natural satellite and has a significant influence on our planet's tides and rotational stability. Its surface is covered in regolith and ancient lava plains, recording billions of years of solar system history without atmospheric erosion. As the only celestial body humans have visited, it remains the primary target for future deep-space exploration and colonization.
ou_involvement: OU analysis of rock samples returned by the Apollo missions helped show that the Moon is not as dry as once thought, and that water is locked inside lunar minerals. Building on instrument experience from missions such as Beagle 2 and Rosetta, OU teams now develop miniature laboratories to measure what the Moon is made of. They also research in-situ resource utilisation: how lunar regolith could supply water, oxygen and fuel, and how it could be used to build on the Moon. This work supports plans for sustainable future exploration of the Moon.

name: Chandrayaan-1
description: Chandrayaan-1 was India's first lunar probe and was instrumental in discovering widespread evidence of water molecules on the Moon. It carried a suite of international instruments to create a detailed three-dimensional map of the lunar surface and its mineral composition. The mission successfully reached lunar orbit and operated for nearly a year before its mission was completed.
ou_involvement: The Centre for Electronic Imaging performed the proton radiation-damage assessment for the C1XS instrument's 24 CCD54 X-ray detectors, using ESA's SPENVIS software to model shielding, operating temperature, and voltage requirements. The team pre-flight characterised 14 candidate detector modules and recommended the ten best-performing units for flight, and continues to provide advisory support on the detectors' in-orbit radiation performance.

name: Chang'e-5
description: Chang'e-5 was a landmark Chinese mission that successfully returned approximately two kilograms of lunar soil and rocks to Earth in late 2020. It targeted a younger region of the Moon called Oceanus Procellarum to provide insights into late-stage lunar volcanic activity. The mission involved a complex series of manoeuvres, including an automated docking in lunar orbit for the return journey.
ou_involvement: In April 2025 the Open University was one of only seven institutions outside China selected to borrow samples from the Chang'e-5 mission. The OU team is using the university's laboratory facilities to determine the isotopic composition of carbon, nitrogen, oxygen, and noble gases within the grains. This research aims to test the giant-impact theory of the Moon's origin and reveal the history of volatiles in the Earth-Moon system.

name: PROSPECT
description: PROSPECT is an ESA package that will drill up to about a metre into the ground near the Moon's south pole and analyse the samples for water ice and other volatiles. It will fly on Intuitive Machines' Nova-C lander (IM-4) under NASA's Commercial Lunar Payload Services programme, with launch planned for 2027. It was first built for Russia's Luna 27 lander, until ESA ended that cooperation in 2022.
ou_involvement: The Open University leads the development of ProSPA, the sample-processing instrument of ESA's PROSPECT lunar-volatiles package. The OU-led team heats and chemically analyses drilled polar samples via mass spectrometry to characterise lunar volatiles such as water ice, supported by STFC RAL Space, Airbus Defence and Space, and German partners at the Max Planck Institute and TU Munich.

name: LUPEX
description: The Lunar Polar Exploration mission is a joint project between ISRO and JAXA designed to search for water ice and other volatiles at the lunar south pole. It will deploy a rover capable of drilling into the lunar surface to collect samples for analysis. The mission is critical for identifying resources that could support future long-term lunar habitation and exploration.
ou_involvement: The Open University is developing the Exploration Mass Spectrometer (EMS-L), an instrument for JAXA's LUPEX rover mission to the lunar south pole, targeted for 2028. The instrument will measure the concentration and type of volatiles released from excavated subsurface material to help assess the Moon's potential for in-situ resource utilisation. This work builds on the OU's established heritage in space-instrument development, including flight hardware for the Rosetta and Beagle 2 missions.

name: Earth-Sun L2
description: Lagrange Point 2 is a point where the pull of the Sun and Earth balances a spacecraft's orbital motion, located approximately 1.5 million kilometers away from the Earth, directly opposite the Sun. It provides a perfect, quiet environment for space telescopes to observe the deep universe without interference from Earth's heat. Spacecraft at this location follow a halo or Lissajous orbit to maintain a constant line of sight for communication.
ou_involvement: The OU uses this reference point as a virtual laboratory to study how deep-space environment conditions affect various satellite components. Academics monitor the performance of multiple OU-characterized missions that are stationed at this critical vantage point. This data is used to improve the design of future detectors for flagship missions currently under development at the university.

name: JWST
description: The James Webb Space Telescope is the premier space observatory of the decade, designed to solve mysteries in our solar system and beyond. It uses a massive gold-coated mirror to capture faint infrared light from the very first stars and galaxies formed after the Big Bang. Since its launch in 2021, it has revolutionized our understanding of exoplanet atmospheres and galactic evolution.
ou_involvement: OU astronomers use JWST to study the atmospheres of planets around other stars. They were part of the international teams that analysed JWST's first detailed observations of the giant planet WASP-39b, which revealed its clouds and chemistry, and OU-funded research has studied the small rocky planet L 98-59 d, where JWST found possible signs of volcanic gases.

name: Gaia
description: Gaia is an ambitious ESA mission designed to create the largest and most precise three-dimensional map of our galaxy. By surveying nearly two billion stars, it provides data on their positions, distances, and motions with incredible accuracy. This massive dataset allows astronomers to reconstruct the history and future of the Milky Way across billions of years.
ou_involvement: The CEI modelled the charge-trapping effects of radiation damage in Gaia's CCD detectors ahead of launch, and has since analysed in-flight data from the BP/RP and RVS radiation campaigns, feeding directly into the mission's data-processing pipeline. In-orbit measurements showed Gaia's detectors accumulating less radiation damage than ground-based testing had predicted, a discrepancy the CEI is still investigating to improve how future missions are radiation-tested before launch. OU PhD students separately use Gaia's vast catalogues to study stellar clusters and binary star systems, and OU researchers use Gaia's science alerts to find transient objects. Gaia is a core case study in the OU's S818 Space Science module, where students use Gaia data to make follow-up observations with the OU's remote telescope in Tenerife.

name: Euclid
description: Euclid is an ESA space telescope designed to investigate the 'Dark Universe' by observing the shapes and distances of billions of galaxies. It maps the structure of the cosmos out to 10 billion light-years to track how dark matter and dark energy influence the expansion of the universe. The mission provides high-resolution imaging that allows scientists to detect the subtle effects of gravitational lensing.
ou_involvement: The CEI played a lead role in characterising the CCD273 detectors for the VIS instrument and developed 'trap pumping', now used in orbit: a method that pinpoints individual radiation-damage defects in the detectors with sub-pixel precision, giving an accurate measure of how the detectors degrade in space so that images can be corrected and kept at science quality. This OU-developed calibration method is essential for correcting the mission's imaging data and preserving the high-precision shape measurements needed to trace dark matter through gravitational lensing. OU astronomers also lead research groups that use Euclid's wide-field surveys to identify rare gravitational lenses.

name: NewAthena
description: NewAthena is a planned ESA X-ray observatory, due for launch around 2037, designed to answer fundamental questions about the 'Hot and Energetic Universe.' It will observe massive black holes, galaxy clusters, and the hot gas that fills the space between galaxies to see how they evolve over time. The telescope will feature a massive collecting area and high-spectral resolution to detect the movement of matter under extreme gravity.
ou_involvement: The CEI is working with institutions around the world on the design and experimental testing of graded-Z shielding for the mission's Wide Field Imager (WFI) instrument, layering high- and low-Z materials to block high-energy particles and the secondary radiation they produce. Researchers use the GEANT4 simulation toolkit, validated against real detector tests, to model how this shielding will perform in orbit before launch.

name: HWO
description: The Habitable Worlds Observatory is a future flagship NASA telescope designed to find and characterize Earth-like planets around other stars. It will use a massive, stable mirror and a coronagraph to block out starlight, allowing it to image faint planets in the habitable zone. The mission's primary goal is to search for biosignatures like oxygen and methane in the atmospheres of distant worlds.
ou_involvement: The CEI is developing high-precision, low-noise UV and photon-counting detectors for HWO's extremely faint imaging tasks, building on the university's CASTOR mission heritage. The OU is also part of the UK consortium that received £3 million in 2026 to develop one of the telescope's core instruments. This long-term research keeps the OU at the forefront of the international search for life beyond our solar system.

name: PLATO
description: PLATO is an upcoming ESA mission designed to detect and characterize Earth-sized exoplanets orbiting bright, Sun-like stars. It will use 26 separate cameras to monitor hundreds of thousands of stars for the tiny dip in brightness caused by a planet passing in front. The mission aims to find worlds in the habitable zone where liquid water could exist on the surface.
ou_involvement: Open University researchers lead population studies to identify and filter out astrophysical false positives (such as blended eclipsing binaries) that could otherwise be mistaken for planets in PLATO's target fields, work supported by UK Space Agency funding for the mission's Development Phase. The team also contributes detector performance, calibration, and radiation-tolerance studies through the university's Centre for Electronic Imaging. The OU's own robotic telescopes could provide follow-up observations of candidate stars once the mission is flying.

name: Roman
description: The Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope will provide a field of view 100 times larger than Hubble's while maintaining the same high-resolution quality. It is designed to perform massive surveys that will help scientists understand dark energy and the distribution of exoplanets in our galaxy. The mission also carries a technology demonstration coronagraph to test new ways of directly imaging planets around other stars.
ou_involvement: CEI researchers at the Open University worked under contract to JPL from 2014 to 2019 to characterise, design and test the EM-CCD sensor for Roman's coronagraph instrument, resulting in the CCD311, a customised, radiation-hardened variant of the CCD201 selected for flight. The team continues to refine the 'trap-pumping' calibration techniques developed for Euclid to mitigate the effects of cosmic radiation on these sensors throughout the mission.

name: Mars
description: Mars is known as the Red Planet due to the iron oxide on its surface and features the largest volcanoes and deepest canyons in the Solar System. Its thin atmosphere and frozen polar caps suggest a world that was once much warmer and wetter billions of years ago. Today, it is the focus of intense robotic exploration as scientists look for signs of ancient microbial life.
ou_involvement: The Open University has a long history of Martian research, ranging from the design of lander instruments to the analysis of orbital atmospheric data. Academics lead research into the planet's volatile cycles and the potential habitability of its subsurface environments. This research is used to support international space agencies in selecting landing sites for future rover and sample return missions.

name: ExoMars TGO
description: The ExoMars Trace Gas Orbiter is an ESA-led mission designed to map the presence of trace gases, like methane, in the Martian atmosphere. It orbits the planet to identify potential biological or geological sources of these gases while studying the atmosphere's composition and structure. The orbiter also serves as a vital communications relay for rovers on the surface, including NASA's Perseverance and Curiosity.
ou_involvement: The Open University designed and led the development of the UVIS ultraviolet channel of the NOMAD spectrometer suite, and an OU planetary scientist serves as a Co-Principal Investigator for NOMAD. The OU also helps operate the CaSSIS stereo imager aboard ExoMars TGO. Researchers at the university use the UVIS data to track ozone, water vapour, and trace gases including methane in the Martian atmosphere, helping to understand how water escapes into space. This work involves international collaboration to validate atmospheric models and support the search for life on the Red Planet.

name: Beagle 2
description: Beagle 2 was a UK-led Mars lander that was deployed from the Mars Express spacecraft in 2003 but failed to transmit data after landing. The spacecraft was thought to be lost until 2015, when high-resolution images from NASA's MRO showed the lander had partially deployed on the Martian surface. It was designed to search for signs of past life by analysing the isotopic composition of carbon in Martian rocks.
ou_involvement: The Beagle 2 mission was conceived and led by an Open University professor, who designed the lander's Gas Analysis Package (GAP): a miniaturised, twelve-oven stepped-combustion mass spectrometer built to detect isotopic signatures of past life in Martian soil. Fitting a laboratory-scale instrument into a probe the size of a dinner plate required major feats of miniaturisation. The OU also led the Environmental Sensor Suite (ESS), designed to measure the weather at the surface of Mars and the presence of dust devils. Though contact with the lander was lost after its 2003 touchdown, the technical lessons learned went on to inform later international planetary landers, including ExoMars.

name: Perseverance
description: Perseverance is NASA's most advanced Mars rover and is currently exploring the Jezero Crater for signs of ancient microbial life. It is equipped with a sophisticated drill and a sample caching system to collect and store Martian rocks for a future return to Earth. The rover also carried the Ingenuity helicopter, which demonstrated the first powered flight on another planet.
ou_involvement: An Open University researcher is part of the international NASA/ESA Mars Sample Return Campaign Science Group advising on which samples collected by Perseverance in Jezero Crater should be prioritised for return to Earth. OU researchers also use the rover's remote sensing and imaging data to study the mineralogy of the ancient river delta, including clay and carbonate minerals linked to past water activity, sharing this research with students through the OU's distance-learning platform.

name: ExoMars Rosalind Franklin
description: The Rosalind Franklin rover is a major ESA mission designed to search for signs of life in the Martian subsurface at Oxia Planum. It features a unique drill that can reach up to two meters underground to collect samples protected from harsh surface radiation. The rover will carry a suite of scientific instruments to analyse the geology, mineralogy, and chemistry of these ancient samples.
ou_involvement: Open University researchers are members of the science team for the rover's PanCam camera system and the Enfys spectrometer. Operations for PanCam and Enfys are also supported from the OU.

name: MSL Curiosity
description: The Mars Science Laboratory, known as Curiosity, is a car-sized rover that has been exploring Gale Crater since 2012. Its primary goal is to determine if Mars ever had an environment capable of supporting microbial life by studying its geology and climate. The mission has successfully identified evidence of ancient freshwater lakes and complex organic molecules on the Martian surface.
ou_involvement: OU academics are members of the Mars Science Laboratory science team, focusing on noble-gas studies and the chemical interactions between Martian rocks and ancient water relevant to habitability. Other OU researchers combine the rover's atmospheric data with ExoMars Trace Gas Orbiter observations to model Mars's dust and water cycles. This work is part of a broader international effort at the OU to understand the long-term habitability of the Red Planet.

name: Jupiter
description: Jupiter is the largest planet in our Solar System and is a massive gas giant famous for its Great Red Spot. It has about a hundred known moons and a faint ring system, serving as a miniature solar system for astronomers to study. Its intense gravity and magnetic field have a profound influence on the movement of objects throughout the outer Solar System.

name: Io
description: Io is the innermost of Jupiter's four large Galilean moons and is the most geologically active body in the Solar System. Its surface is constantly reshaped by hundreds of volcanoes, which are fueled by the intense tidal heating caused by Jupiter's gravity. The moon's yellow-orange color is a result of the sulfur and sulfur dioxide frost that covers its entire surface.

name: Europa
description: Europa is an icy moon of Jupiter that is believed to hide a massive liquid water ocean beneath its frozen crust. Its smooth surface is crisscrossed by cracks and streaks, suggesting that the ice shell is dynamic and relatively young. Scientists consider Europa one of the best candidates in the Solar System for finding habitable environments beyond Earth.
ou_involvement: Open University astrobiologists research Europa as one of the Solar System's most promising 'ocean worlds', developing novel cryo-analytical laboratory techniques and planetary simulation facilities to study icy surface materials at the molecular and micro-scale. Fieldwork in polar environments such as the Canadian High Arctic helps researchers understand how ice and salts delivered to the surface by cryovolcanism can reveal what conditions exist in the ocean far below.

name: Ganymede
description: Ganymede is the largest moon in the Solar System and is even bigger than the planet Mercury. It is the only known moon to possess its own magnetic field, which creates brilliant aurorae around its poles. The moon features a mix of dark, cratered regions and lighter, grooved terrain that indicates a complex geological history.
ou_involvement: Ganymede is one of the icy 'ocean worlds' studied by Open University astrobiologists, whose research develops cryo-analytical lab techniques and planetary-simulation facilities to analyse the ice and salts that reach such moons' surfaces via cryovolcanism. This research aims to reveal the chemistry of the vast subsurface ocean thought to lie beneath Ganymede's ice shell, complementing the OU's separate technical contribution to the JUICE mission that will study the moon directly.

name: Callisto
description: Callisto is the most heavily cratered object in the Solar System and shows very few signs of geological activity on its ancient surface. It is composed of equal parts rock and ice and may also contain a subsurface ocean deep within its interior. Its distance from Jupiter means it is less affected by the planet's intense radiation environment compared to the other Galilean moons.

name: JUICE
description: The JUpiter ICy moons Explorer is a major ESA mission launched in 2023 to investigate the habitability of Jupiter's large moons. It is currently cruising through the solar system and will arrive at Jupiter in 2031 to perform detailed studies of Ganymede, Europa, and Callisto. The mission aims to understand how habitable environments could arise around gas giant planets in the outer Solar System.
ou_involvement: The Open University's Centre for Electronic Imaging, working with detector manufacturer Teledyne e2v, developed and characterised the CIS115 CMOS image sensor at the heart of the JANUS camera system, testing it against the intense radiation, vibration and thermal extremes of the journey to Jupiter. The OU is the UK National Lead for the JANUS instrument.

name: Saturn
description: Saturn is a massive gas giant famous for its spectacular ring system, which is composed primarily of ice and rock particles. It is the second-largest planet in the Solar System and has a diverse collection of hundreds of moons, including the massive, orange-hued Titan. Despite its great size, the planet has a very low density and would theoretically float if placed in a large enough ocean.
ou_involvement: OU researchers have studied dust in the Saturn system with Cassini's Cosmic Dust Analyser, helping to calibrate the instrument and analysing the composition of dust around the planet. An OU scientist also led the Surface Science Package on the Huygens probe, which landed on Titan, Saturn's largest moon.

name: Titan
description: Titan is the largest moon of Saturn and the only moon in the Solar System to possess a thick atmosphere and liquid lakes on its surface. These lakes are composed of liquid methane and ethane, creating a weather cycle similar to Earth's but at much colder temperatures. Its thick, orange haze hides a complex surface that features vast dunes, mountains, and potentially even cryovolcanoes.
ou_involvement: Titan's first global geomorphological map, published in Nature Astronomy in 2019, used Cassini data to identify six major terrain types across the moon's surface, from plains to dune fields. Titan is also one of the icy 'ocean worlds' studied by OU astrobiologists, whose research explores how its surface chemistry and methane cycle could relate to conditions for life. This body-focused research sits alongside the OU's separate instrument-development work on the Cassini and Huygens missions.

name: Cassini
description: The Cassini-Huygens mission was a landmark international collaboration that spent 13 years exploring the Saturnian system in incredible detail. It discovered active geysers on the moon Enceladus and provided our first clear views of Titan's surface through its thick atmosphere. The mission concluded in 2017 with a deliberate plunge into Saturn's atmosphere to protect its moons from contamination.
ou_involvement: OU planetary scientists utilized Cassini's extensive datasets to conduct world-leading research on the habitability and chemistry of Saturn's icy moons. OU researchers helped calibrate Cassini's Cosmic Dust Analyser and studied the composition of dust around Saturn. This research continues today as the university uses Cassini's archival data to train students in planetary science and data interpretation.

name: Huygens
description: The Huygens probe was an ESA spacecraft that performed the first and only landing in the outer Solar System on Saturn's moon Titan in 2005. It successfully transmitted data and images during its two-hour descent through the moon's thick nitrogen-rich atmosphere. The landing revealed a world of riverbeds and rounded pebbles that were shaped by the flow of liquid methane.
ou_involvement: The Open University was the Principal Investigator for the Surface Science Package (SSP), which recorded the first-ever in situ data from the surface of Titan, measuring its density, temperature and physical state on impact. OU academics have continued to lead analysis of this historic dataset to understand Titan's surface properties and organic chemistry.

name: Uranus
description: Uranus is an ice giant planet that is uniquely characterized by its extreme axial tilt, causing it to rotate almost on its side. Its pale blue-green color is a result of the methane in its atmosphere, which absorbs red light and reflects blue and green. It features a faint ring system and a diverse family of 29 known moons, most of which are composed of ice and rock.

name: Rosetta
description: The Rosetta mission was a ground-breaking ESA project that performed the first successful long-term study of a comet's nucleus. It orbited Comet 67P for over two years, observing its transformation as it travelled through the inner Solar System. The mission provided unprecedented data on the physical and chemical properties of comets and their role in the origin of life.
ou_involvement: The Open University co-developed the Ptolemy gas-analysis instrument on the Philae lander with RAL Space to measure the isotopic composition of cometary carbon, nitrogen and oxygen. OU scientists also contributed to the MUPUS surface-properties instrument and the GIADA dust analyser, and coordinated the mission's international ground-based observing campaign. Other OU research has explored why comet 67P's dust and gas jets follow a day-night cycle as it approaches the Sun.

name: Philae
description: Philae was the robotic lander carried by the Rosetta spacecraft and became the first mission to land successfully on a comet's nucleus in 2014. It carried a suite of ten instruments designed to perform in-situ analysis of the comet's surface and subsurface materials. Despite a bounce during landing, it successfully transmitted data back to Earth before entering hibernation.
ou_involvement: Together with RAL Space, the OU designed and built the Ptolemy gas analyser, which with the COSAC instrument made the first chemical analysis of the organic matter found on a comet's surface. Academics at the university lead the interpretation of this data to search for the chemical building blocks of life. This involvement has established the OU as a world leader in miniaturized planetary laboratory technology and cometary science.

name: Hera
description: Hera is an ESA planetary defence mission launched in 2024 to investigate the binary asteroid system Didymos and its moon Dimorphos. It will study the results of NASA's DART mission, which successfully impacted Dimorphos to demonstrate a kinetic deflection technique. The spacecraft will characterize the crater and the asteroid's internal structure to help refine our planetary defence strategies.
ou_involvement: Open University researchers were on the Hera Science Team's management board.

name: AKARI
description: AKARI was a Japanese infrared astronomy satellite that performed an all-sky survey at various infrared wavelengths. It was designed to study the formation and evolution of stars and galaxies across the history of the universe. The mission produced high-quality catalogs that continue to be a vital resource for astronomers worldwide.
ou_involvement: The Open University was one of the international partner institutes on JAXA's AKARI infrared satellite, alongside Nagoya University, the University of Tokyo, ESA and other UK institutions. OU researchers used AKARI's all-sky infrared survey and near-infrared spectroscopy to study interstellar dust, polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons, and the earliest stages of star formation in galaxies, work that helps build a clearer picture of the cosmic chemical cycle that eventually leads to habitable worlds.

name: Spitzer
description: The Spitzer Space Telescope was one of NASA's Great Observatories and was optimized for observing the infrared universe. It made numerous high-profile discoveries, including the detection of the TRAPPIST-1 system's Earth-sized exoplanets. The mission operated for over 16 years, providing our clearest views of planet-forming disks and distant, dusty galaxies.
ou_involvement: OU scientists analyze Spitzer's archival light curves to characterize the atmospheres and orbits of transiting exoplanets. Academics at the university use this data to teach students about infrared astronomy and the search for habitable worlds. This research remains a core component of the OU's astronomy research and is used to inform the target selection for new missions like Ariel.

name: Herschel
description: Herschel was the largest infrared telescope launched until JWST and was designed to study the coolest objects in the universe. It observed the formation of stars and galaxies across cosmic time and provided our first clear detection of water molecules in star-forming regions. The mission's huge mirror and sensitive detectors allowed it to peer through dust that blocks visible light.
ou_involvement: The Open University's astronomy group used data from SPIRE, the camera and spectrometer built for Herschel by an international consortium led by Cardiff University. Academics at the university lead research into sub-millimetre observations of distant galaxies to study the history of star formation. This heritage in infrared instrumentation is used today to train the next generation of space engineers and astronomers.

name: Planck
description: The Planck mission was an ESA satellite designed to map the Cosmic Microwave Background (CMB) with unprecedented precision. It captured the oldest light in the universe, providing a detailed 'baby picture' of the cosmos just 380,000 years after the Big Bang. The mission's data has been essential for refining our understanding of the universe's age, composition, and expansion rate.
ou_involvement: OU researchers use Planck's high-resolution maps of the cosmic microwave background to study the large-scale structure of the early universe and the distribution of galaxy clusters. The university's cosmology group contributes to research into dark matter and dark energy that draws on Planck's data alongside more recent missions like Euclid. This work provides a fundamental framework for teaching cosmology and the history of the universe at the Open University.

name: Peregrine
description: Peregrine was a US commercial lunar lander developed by Astrobotic but suffered a propellant leak shortly after its launch in early 2024. Despite the leak, the team successfully operated several scientific payloads in deep space before the spacecraft re-entered Earth's atmosphere. It was intended to demonstrate a new low-cost delivery service to the lunar surface for commercial and scientific customers.
ou_involvement: The Open University, working with STFC RAL Space under ESA contract, developed the Exospheric Mass Spectrometer (PITMS) to make the first in-situ measurements of the lunar exosphere. Although a propulsion failure meant Peregrine never landed, OU researchers kept the instrument running throughout its unplanned journey through deep space, demonstrating full functionality and returning valuable engineering and calibration data. This work has directly informed the design of more robust spectrometers for upcoming lunar landing missions.

name: Comet Interceptor
description: Comet Interceptor is a unique ESA mission designed to 'ambush' a pristine comet that is entering the inner Solar System for the first time. It will wait at the Earth-Sun L2 point for a suitable target to be discovered by new surveys before being deployed to perform a flyby. The mission aims to study a comet that has never been altered by the Sun's heat, providing a clear look at early Solar System material.
ou_involvement: The Open University's School of Physical Sciences is a Co-Investigator institution for the DISC dust impact instrument, which will measure the size, mass and velocity of cometary dust particles during the spacecraft's high-speed flyby. The university operates a Light-Gas Gun facility, firing particles at several kilometres per second to verify the instrument's dust shield can survive real hypervelocity impacts.

name: EnVision
description: EnVision is a planned ESA orbiter mission designed to provide a comprehensive look at Venus' surface geology and atmospheric dynamics. It will feature high-resolution radar and specialized spectrometers to see through the planet's thick clouds and search for signs of active volcanism. The mission aims to determine if Venus was once a habitable planet with liquid water oceans and plate tectonics.
ou_involvement: The Open University's Atmospheric Research and Space Exploration group leads the testing and characterisation of the UV detectors for the VenSpec-U instrument, part of the VenSpec suite, funded by a £2.3 million ESA grant. The team also takes part in science preparations for the mission ahead of launch in the early 2030s.

name: LightShip-1
description: ESA’s LightShip-1 is an innovative electric-propulsion tug designed to deliver spacecraft directly into Mars orbit. Once its primary delivery mission is complete, the spacecraft will establish the Mars Communication and Navigation Infrastructure (MARCONI) while also engaging in exploration science through its onboard instruments.
ou_involvement: The Open University’s Atmospheric Research and Space Exploration group is leading the design phase for the High-Resolution Imager for Mars Exploration (HiRIME) telescope carried by LightShip. The OU’s work is critical to delivering high-resolution imagery of the Martian surface for planetary geology. The same group also leads the Dust Environment Spectral Imager instrument on LightShip, which will take global images of Mars about every 10 minutes to monitor the global atmosphere and dust storms.

name: OGRE
description: The Off-plane Grating Rocket Experiment is a sub-orbital sounding rocket mission designed to capture the highest-resolution X-ray spectra of stellar sources. It will be launched from a rocket to fly above the Earth's atmosphere for several minutes of precise observations before returning to the ground. The mission aims to study the hot and energetic gas around stars and galaxies to understand their chemical evolution.
ou_involvement: The CEI characterises and optimises the four EM-CCD sensors in OGRE's X-ray camera, which is built by the UK company XCAM, engineered to survive the violent vibrations of a rocket launch. Academics at the university lead research into radiation damage, charge transfer efficiency, and the use of these high-speed detectors for photon counting in the soft X-ray regime. This work is part of a broader OU initiative to develop new technologies for high-energy astrophysics and stellar research.

name: Hayabusa2
description: Hayabusa2 was a Japanese mission that successfully deployed multiple rovers and returned samples from the near-Earth asteroid Ryugu. It used a series of innovative techniques, including a kinetic impactor, to collect material from both the surface and subsurface of the asteroid. The mission provided invaluable insights into the composition of carbon-rich asteroids and the history of the early Solar System.
ou_involvement: The Open University's oxygen isotope laboratory was one of the international groups invited to join "Team Kochi," one of the three Japanese-led initial analysis teams for the returned Ryugu samples. OU researchers are using the university's laboratory facilities to measure oxygen isotopes in the grains, showing that Ryugu-like material may have delivered water to the early Earth.

name: OSIRIS-REx
description: OSIRIS-REx was a NASA mission that successfully collected a massive sample of rocks and dust from the carbon-rich asteroid Bennu. It returned the samples to Earth in late 2023, providing scientists with pristine material that dates back to the very beginning of our Solar System. The spacecraft has since been renamed OSIRIS-APEX and is now on a new mission to study the asteroid Apophis in 2029.
ou_involvement: OU researchers worked with NASA's OSIRIS-REx team to help select Bennu's Nightingale sample site, producing detailed temperature predictions to ensure the spacecraft and its samples didn't overheat during collection. Open University academics are also involved in analysing the returned Bennu material to investigate the early Solar System's chemistry and the origin of Earth's water and organic molecules.

name: Stardust
description: Stardust was the first mission designed to collect and return samples from a comet's coma and interstellar dust to Earth. It used a unique silica aerogel collector to capture the tiny particles at high speeds without destroying them during the encounter. The mission's return capsule successfully landed in 2006, providing the first clear look at cometary material in a laboratory.
ou_involvement: OU researchers were among the first scientists worldwide to analyse material from the Stardust mission, using infrared, UV/visible and Raman spectroscopy to study the mineralogy of dust grains captured from Comet Wild 2 in the aerogel collector. This work, alongside studies of the sample's organic content, helped establish the OU as a leading UK centre for cometary sample science.

name: Bennu
description: Bennu is a diamond-shaped, carbon-rich near-Earth asteroid that is believed to contain primitive material from the birth of our Solar System. Its surface is covered in loose rocks and dust, suggesting it is a 'rubble pile' held together by very weak gravity. The asteroid is a primary target for scientists who are looking to understand the role of asteroids in delivering life's building blocks to Earth.

name: Ryugu
description: Ryugu is a dark, diamond-shaped asteroid that has an orbit that crosses Earth's and is composed primarily of carbon-rich material. Its low density and porous structure indicate that it is a rubble-pile asteroid with significant void spaces in its interior. The asteroid's surface features a mix of large boulders and fine dust, recording a complex history of impacts and space weathering.

name: Didymos
description: Didymos is a near-Earth asteroid about 780 metres across, orbited by a moonlet about 150 metres across called Dimorphos. In September 2022 NASA's DART spacecraft deliberately crashed into Dimorphos and shortened its orbit around Didymos by about 33 minutes, the first test of moving an asteroid. ESA's Hera mission arrives in late 2026 to measure exactly what the impact did.

name: Comet Wild 2
description: Comet Wild 2 is a periodic comet that features a lumpy, cratered nucleus and was the first comet to have its dust sampled and returned to Earth. Its surface is surprisingly rugged, with steep-walled depressions and flat-bottomed craters that suggest a complex geological structure. The comet is composed of ancient material that has remained largely frozen since the formation of the Solar System.

name: Comet 67P
description: Comet 67P/Churyumov–Gerasimenko is a Jupiter-family comet that features a distinct 'rubber duck' shape with two large lobes connected by a neck. It has a very low density and is composed primarily of dust, water ice, and frozen gases like carbon dioxide. The comet's active surface produces spectacular jets of dust and gas as it approaches the heat of the Sun.

name: 4731 MonicaGrady
description: A main-belt asteroid named after planetary scientist Monica Grady. Monica is Emeritus Professor at the Open University, and curator of the meteorite collection at the Natural History Museum in London, she studies carbon isotopes in a wide range of meteorites with a focus on understanding the geologic processes leading to their formation. She is also actively involved in meteorite recovery efforts around the world. The shape model of this object is awaiting further study - and it may or may not be accurately represented in this visualisation.

name: 20386 IanFranchi
description: A main-belt asteroid named in honor of Ian Franchi. Ian is a British cosmochemist and emeritus professor at The Open University. He has forty years experience studying the origin and evolution of the early Solar System using advanced analytical techniques, and in particular, high-precision oxygen isotope measurements, on extraterrestrial materials. The shape model of this object is awaiting further study - and it may or may not be accurately represented in this visualisation.

name: 20617 RichardGreenwood
description: A main-belt asteroid honoring Richard Greenwood. Richard is an English senior research fellow at The Open University who specializes in using oxygen isotopic analyses of extraterrestrial material to understand the origin and early evolution of the Solar System. He has also written a book on meteorites that was geared towards a general audience. The shape model of this object is awaiting further study - and it may or may not be accurately represented in this visualisation.

name: 20626 Rider-Stokes
description: A main-belt asteroid honoring Ben Rider-Stokes. Ben is an English post-doctoral researcher at The Open University specializing in understanding the timing of magmatic differentiation and volatile accretion of achondrites. He evaluates the spectral characteristics of meteorites in the ultraviolet, visible, and near-infrared to identify meteoritic analogs for asteroids. The shape model of this object is awaiting further study - and it may or may not be accurately represented in this visualisation.

name: 69423 OpenUni
description: Named in honor of the Open University. The Open University (founded 1969 April 23) is the world’s leading university for flexible, innovative distance learning, having educated over 2 million part-time students. Through its research in astronomy, planetary and space science, the OU has a distinguished history of involvement in major Solar System exploration missions. The shape model of this object is awaiting further study - and it may or may not be accurately represented in this visualisation.

name: 10230 AndrewNorton
description: A main-belt asteroid honoring Andrew Norton. Andrew is an English astrophysicist and was Professor at the Open University where he led major teaching and outreach initiatives, and carried out research into the time-domain astrophysics of compact binary stars. He led the SuperWASP Variable Stars citizen science project, supervised numerous Ph.D. students and won the RAS Higher Education Award. The shape model of this object is awaiting further study - and it may or may not be accurately represented in this visualisation.

name: 9831 SimonGreen
description: A main-belt asteroid honoring Simon Green. Simon is Emeritus Professor at the Open University and has carried out observations of minor planets and transneptunian objects for over 20 years, starting with the use of the IRAS satellite to detect fast-moving objects. The shape model of this object is awaiting further study - and it may or may not be accurately represented in this visualisation.

name: 15614 Pillinger
description: Named in honor of Colin Pillinger. Colin was a Professor at the Open University and a planetary geochemist who made significant discoveries in the light-element geochemistry of meteorites, diamonds, lunar samples and terrestrial samples. He was the originator and principal investigator of the Beagle 2 Mars lander. The shape model of this object is awaiting further study - and it may or may not be accurately represented in this visualisation.

name: 20594 Pemartin
description: A main-belt asteroid honoring Pierre-Etienne Martin. Pierre-Etienne is a French planetary scientist and research fellow at the Open University, investigating micron- to submicron-sized inclusions in Martian and carbonaceous meteorites (CMs). During his Ph.D., he studied refractory inclusions to assess aqueous alteration in CMs and joined the Hayabusa2 returned-samples analysis team. The shape model of this object is awaiting further study - and it may or may not be accurately represented in this visualisation.

name: 17920 Zarnecki
description: Named in honor of space scientist John Zarnecki. While at The Open University, he developed spacecraft instrumentation to study the surfaces and atmospheres of planets, satellites and small bodies. He was a PI for the Huygens probe/lander on the Cassini mission to Saturn and Saturn VI (Titan). John has also served as a Director of the International Space Science Institute. The shape model of this object is awaiting further study - and it may or may not be accurately represented in this visualisation.

name: Earth-Sun L1
description: Lagrange Point 1 is a point where the pull of the Sun and Earth balances a spacecraft's orbital motion, located approximately 1.5 million kilometers away from the Earth, directly between our planet and the Sun. It provides a constant, uninterrupted view of the Sun, making it the ideal location for solar monitoring satellites. Spacecraft at this point are essential for providing early warnings of solar flares and geomagnetic storms that could impact Earth.

name: Genesis
description: Genesis was a NASA mission that spent over two years at the Earth-Sun L1 point collecting samples of the solar wind to analyse the Sun's composition. It used specialized collector arrays to capture individual solar particles before returning them to Earth in a sample return capsule. Despite a hard landing in Utah, the mission successfully provided the first precise measurements of the Sun's oxygen and nitrogen isotopes.
ou_involvement: Genesis showed that the Sun is richer in oxygen-16 than the Earth, Moon, Mars and meteorites. This is a key reference point for OU research on oxygen isotopes in meteorites and returned samples.

name: Ariel
description: Ariel is a planned ESA mission designed to perform the first large-scale survey of the chemical composition of exoplanet atmospheres. It will observe over a thousand diverse worlds in visible and infrared wavelengths to understand how planets form and evolve across the galaxy. The mission aims to find links between the atmospheres of planets and their parent stars and host environments.

name: Open Science Observatories
description: The Open Science Observatories consist of two robotic telescopes, PIRATE and COAST, located at the Teide Observatory in Tenerife. They are designed to be operated remotely by students and researchers from anywhere in the world through a web-based interface. The facility is used for both undergraduate teaching and professional astronomical research, including the search for transiting exoplanets.
ou_involvement: The telescopes are owned and operated by the Open University and serve as a cornerstone of its distance-learning astronomy curriculum. Academics use the facility to conduct long-term monitoring of variable stars and to provide ground-based support for international space missions like Ariel. This unique educational resource allows students to gain real-world experience in astronomical data collection and analysis.

name: Mars Yard
description: The Mars Yard is a specialized planetary simulation facility located on the Open University's campus in Milton Keynes, UK. It features a large area filled with regolith simulant and obstacles designed to mimic the challenging terrain found on the Martian surface. The site is used for autonomous rover testing, including navigation algorithms, and to train future planetary mission operators.
ou_involvement: The facility is integrated into the university's teaching program, allowing students to operate robotic rovers across a simulated Martian landscape from their own homes. This innovative teaching tool is part of the OU's broad commitment to making space science accessible and interactive for a global audience.
